title: Broadcasting semi-classical music with Bowles, Curl and Eddie Barrow
summary: The four-piece Bowles group broadcast three times a week for Howard's Clothing Company, playing semi-classical pieces such as 'Nola', probably the first Black band to do commercial radio in Boston.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Hey, we're gettin' a lit bit away from Boston, I think we should try to clear - why don't you tell the story, soup to nuts, of you and Harry Carney in Boston in the early '20's?
How you met him, how you got involved, and what, the whole deal.

Well, that Harry Carney deal, see, came in from me broadcastin' three days a week with Curl, see. And we were doing mostly technical solo work, I mean, it wasn't so much jazz much, it was semi-classical stuff. I give you an idea - I was playin' things like "Nola" on the saxophone, alto, and Curl was playin' some of those things that he learned in school, I mean those classical trumpet solos, you know, triple tongue, double tongue, all that stuff. And we had the son of Bowles was a drummer, he was singin'. But he sing, he sung ballads, no jazz, he never did bother with much jazz. He was singin' popular songs from the shows, things like that. He always did, see, he was -
He was a guy who played the banjo -
And he had a band, a black band that's playing semi-classical music on -
Well, at that time [ ], that was near and about the end of before I came back, left -

Yeah, somethin' like that. Anyway he, we were - I tell you what we were doing. We were playing for Howard's Clothing Company, the same Howard Clothing Company that you have in New York - I don't think you have it, I believe they closed it, I haven't seen in - you remember the Howard's Clothing Company.

That's what we were playing for, it's a commercial deal. We were the first negroes to ever do that in Boston, or in Massachusetts - maybe in the country, tell you the truth, real commercial. And we had it for a long time, three times a week. And we were playing only classic, semi-classic. And if we did play anything, we'd play it for the drummer, a little background for him to sing, one of those show numbers like -
What was, you don't remember either of their first names?
No, I forget his first name now.
And Langston Curl is, and who else, how many - what was the instrumentation?
I don't know who - he was drummer, Bowles's son -
It was Bowles' son on drums, and Bowles was on banjo?

And the piano player was named, a name like Beryl, Beryl, somethin' like that, Eddie Beryls, somethin' like that, a little semi-classical pianist that could play jazz. It wasn't considered a jazz band like Skinny Johnson and all those guys -

Semi, semi, like my wife - he could play anything, read anything, and it had a little semi - he knew all of the songs and right harmony, see. I think his name Eddie Barrow, Barrow was his name, last name.
B-A-R-R-O-W (BW joins on last three letters) -

Yeah, that's it. So that's the type stuff that we used to do. A lot of people don't know about that because, particularly in New York because wasn't nobody doing, wasn't no negroes doin' that. And that's where I got the pupils, you know I - and that's where I got, I got the pupils from that. I got calls like that and letters from Carney and different, and one - and after I get one, it's easy to get others. Like I told you about my brother workin' in those 2, 3 different bands up there.
